title: Cameras for Everyone, Everywhere
summary: In the 1900s, cameras shrank until they fit in a pocket, flashes lit up dark rooms, and a new camera could print a photo in about a minute. Photographers used pictures to help stop children working in factories, and astronauts photographed the whole Earth from space.

sections.heading: A Camera Small Enough for a Coat Pocket
paragraphs: At the start of the 1900s, serious cameras were still big. Many photographers used wooden or metal cameras with glass plates or large sheets of film, often on a tripod. Even folding cameras for amateurs were bulky. If you wanted to photograph a street scene quietly, without everyone turning to stare, you had a problem.

In the small German town of Wetzlar, an engineer named Oskar Barnack worked for Ernst Leitz, a company famous for microscopes. Barnack loved hiking and photography, and the story often told is that he wanted a camera light enough to carry on long walks. Around 1913 to 1914 he built a small metal prototype, now called the Ur-Leica, meaning the original Leica. His clever idea was to borrow film from the movie industry. Cinema film was 35 millimeters wide, with sprocket holes along both edges, and it was made in huge quantities, so it was cheap and easy to get.

In a movie camera, each frame sits across the film strip. Barnack turned it sideways, running the film horizontally and making each picture twice as big as a movie frame: 24 by 36 millimeters. That size, with a shape of 2 by 3, is still called full frame by photographers today, even on digital cameras. A single roll could take dozens of pictures before reloading. The tiny negative was then enlarged onto paper to make a bigger print.

World War I and hard economic times delayed things, but in 1924 the company boss, Ernst Leitz II, decided to manufacture Barnack's camera anyway. It was shown to the public at the Leipzig Spring Fair in 1925 as the Leica, a name made from the first letters of LEItz and CAmera. Its sharp little lens and quiet shutter changed what photography could be.

With a Leica in hand, a photographer could move through a crowd, catch a child jumping over a puddle or a worker laughing at a café table, and never be noticed. This is called candid photography, meaning natural pictures of people who are not posing. The French photographer Henri Cartier-Bresson became famous for using a small Leica to catch what he called the decisive moment, the split second when everything in a scene comes together. War photographers like Robert Capa carried small 35mm cameras into battle. Soon other companies built 35mm cameras too, and by the 1960s and 1970s Japanese brands such as Nikon and Canon made 35mm the most popular film size in the world.

There is also a brave story connected to the Leica company. After the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, Ernst Leitz II quietly helped many Jewish employees and others leave the country by sending them to work in Leitz sales offices abroad. This effort, later called the Leica Freedom Train, only became widely known after his death.

sections.heading: Lighting Up the Dark: From Flash Powder to Flashbulbs
paragraphs: Film needs light. Outdoors on a sunny day, that is easy. But what about inside a dark room, at night, or in a gloomy alley? In the 1860s, some photographers burned ribbons of magnesium metal, which glows with a brilliant white light, but it was smoky and slow. Then, in 1887, two German scientists, Adolf Miethe and Johannes Gaedicke, introduced flash powder, a mixture of powdered magnesium and a chemical called potassium chlorate that burns in an instant.

Using flash powder was dramatic and dangerous. A photographer poured the powder into a metal tray held high above the head, opened the camera shutter, and then lit the powder. There was a blinding bang of light, a cloud of white smoke, and often a smell of burning. Too much powder could burn hands, singe eyebrows or even start fires, and there were serious accidents. But for the first time, photographers could take pictures in places where the sun never reached.

One of the first people to use flash powder to change the world was Jacob Riis, a Danish immigrant who had arrived in New York in 1870 and become a police reporter. Riis knew the city's crowded tenements, cheap apartment buildings where poor families, many of them immigrants, were packed into dark, airless rooms. Words alone did not seem to move wealthy readers. After reading about flash powder in 1887, Riis and some friends began going into the slums at night to photograph what they found. People were sometimes startled awake by the flash. In 1890 he published a book, How the Other Half Lives, which combined his writing with pictures of the slums.

Riis's work helped push New York to clear one of its worst slums, Mulberry Bend, and turn it into a park in 1897, and it impressed Theodore Roosevelt, then the city's police commissioner, who became his friend. Historians today also point out that Riis's writing included unfair stereotypes about some immigrant groups, a reminder that even reformers can carry the prejudices of their time.

Flash powder was finally replaced by something much safer: the flashbulb. Commercial flashbulbs went on sale in Germany in 1929 and spread around the world in the early 1930s. A flashbulb was a glass bulb filled with oxygen and thin metal foil or wire, first magnesium or aluminum, later zirconium. A small electric current set off the metal inside, which burned in a brilliant flash within the sealed glass. No smoke, no loose powder. The bulb could be used only once, and photographers swapped hot used bulbs between shots. In 1965 Kodak introduced the Flashcube, a little cube with four bulbs that rotated after each picture, so family photographers could take four flash shots in a row.

sections.heading: Doc Edgerton Freezes Time
paragraphs: A flashbulb's light lasted a fraction of a second, short enough for a portrait but far too long to freeze a hummingbird's wings or a bullet in flight. To stop really fast motion, you need light that switches on and off almost instantly. That was the specialty of Harold Edgerton, an engineer at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in Cambridge, Massachusetts, whom students nicknamed Doc and later Papa Flash.

Edgerton grew up in Nebraska and arrived at MIT as a graduate student in the 1920s. He was studying electric motors and wanted to see how their spinning parts behaved. In 1931 he developed a new kind of electronic flash: a glass tube filled with gas that, when a big jolt of stored electricity passed through it, lit up in an extremely short, bright flash. Unlike a flashbulb, it could flash again and again, very quickly and very precisely. A device that flashes rapidly like this is called a stroboscope, or strobe.

With his strobe, Edgerton could make a flash lasting only a tiny fraction of a thousandth of a second, and for some special pictures less than a millionth of a second. Suddenly, things too fast for the human eye could be seen frozen in a photograph. He photographed a hummingbird in flight in 1936, its wings sharp instead of blurred. He photographed a golf club smashing into a ball, flattening it for an instant. His famous picture Milk Drop Coronet (1957) shows a drop of milk splashing into a thin layer of milk and bouncing up in a perfect crown with little beads around the rim. In 1964 he photographed a bullet tearing through an apple, with the fruit exploding on both sides.

Edgerton's strobes were not just for beautiful pictures. They helped engineers study machines, and during World War II his giant flashes helped with nighttime aerial photography. He also helped build special high-speed cameras for studying nuclear tests, worked on underwater cameras and sonar with the ocean explorer Jacques Cousteau, and won an Academy Award for a short film called Quicker'n a Wink (1940). The electronic flash units that clip onto cameras today, and the strobe lights at concerts and on emergency vehicles, all owe a debt to Edgerton's work.

sections.heading: Pictures That Changed Laws
paragraphs: Imagine a girl about ten years old, standing barefoot beside a row of enormous spinning machines in a cotton mill, her hair tied back so it will not get caught. She works long hours, and she is so small she can barely reach the threads. In the early 1900s, scenes like this were common in the United States. Children worked in mills, coal mines, canneries, glass factories and fields, and on city streets selling newspapers. Many people knew about it, but few had really looked.

Lewis Hine made them look. Born in Oshkosh, Wisconsin, in 1874, Hine became a teacher at the Ethical Culture School in New York, where he started using a camera with his students. Between 1904 and 1909 he photographed immigrants arriving at Ellis Island, and he came to believe that a photograph could be a powerful tool for making society fairer. He called his kind of work social photography.

From 1908 Hine worked for the National Child Labor Committee, a group campaigning to end child labor. Factory owners did not want photographers inside, so Hine sometimes pretended to be a fire inspector, a postcard seller or a Bible salesman to get through the gate. He was threatened by factory guards and foremen more than once. Hine was careful to collect facts as well as pictures. He wrote down names, ages and working hours, and he is said to have estimated children's heights by noting which button of his own coat or vest they came up to. That way, no one could claim his pictures were exaggerated.

Over the years he traveled tens of thousands of miles and made thousands of photographs: young boys called breaker boys sorting coal in dusty mines, girls in textile mills, children shucking oysters before dawn. His pictures appeared in pamphlets, posters, magazines and exhibitions. They helped build public support for child labor laws. A national law in 1916 was struck down by the Supreme Court, and the fight went on for years, but in 1938 the Fair Labor Standards Act finally set nationwide limits on child labor in the United States. Hine himself did not grow rich. He struggled for work in the Great Depression and died in poverty in 1940, but his photographs are now treasured collections in museums and the Library of Congress.

sections.heading: Life Magazine and the Migrant Mother
paragraphs: In the 1930s, printing presses could finally reproduce photographs cheaply and beautifully on large pages, and small 35mm cameras let photographers capture real life as it happened. Together, these made a new kind of journalism possible: photojournalism, telling news stories mostly through pictures.

On 23 November 1936, the American publisher Henry Luce launched Life, a weekly magazine built around photographs. It cost ten cents. The first cover showed a huge concrete dam at Fort Peck, Montana, photographed by Margaret Bourke-White, one of the first women photojournalists to become famous. The first issue sold about 380,000 copies, and within four months Life was selling over a million copies a week. In the years that followed, Life photographers such as Robert Capa, Alfred Eisenstaedt and Gordon Parks brought war, science, sports, famous people and ordinary lives into millions of living rooms. Before television news, Life was how many families saw the world.

The Great Depression, which began in 1929, threw millions of Americans out of work. On top of that, a terrible drought in the 1930s turned parts of the Great Plains into the Dust Bowl. Many farming families packed their belongings and drove to California, hoping to find work picking crops. The US government's Resettlement Administration, later called the Farm Security Administration (FSA), hired photographers to record how these families were living, partly to build support for programs to help them.

One of those photographers was Dorothea Lange, who had run a portrait studio in San Francisco before turning her camera on the streets. In March 1936, driving home after a long trip, she passed a sign for a pea pickers' camp near Nipomo, California. She later wrote that she drove on for miles, then turned around and went back. The pea crop had frozen, so there was little work. In the camp, she found a mother with her children sheltering in a tent. Lange later said she stayed only about ten minutes and made a handful of exposures, moving closer each time.

The best-known picture shows the mother gazing into the distance with a worried, tired face, her hand raised to her chin, two children leaning their heads on her shoulders with their faces turned away, and a baby on her lap. It became known as Migrant Mother, and it is one of the most famous photographs ever taken, a symbol of the hardship of the Great Depression. Lange even retouched the negative to remove the mother's thumb, which had appeared in a corner of the frame.

For decades the woman's name was not widely known. In the 1970s a journalist traced her: she was Florence Owens Thompson, a mother of several children with Cherokee roots, who had worked hard all her life. Her feelings about the picture were complicated. For years she was unhappy that her image had been printed so many times while her family stayed poor, and she said Lange had not asked her name. Later, her children came to speak more warmly about the photograph. Her story is a reminder that every famous photo of a person is also a picture of a real human being, with her own life and feelings.

sections.heading: Why Can't I See It Now? The Polaroid
paragraphs: In the 1940s, taking a photograph meant waiting. You finished the roll, took it to a shop, and days later you got your prints back, sometimes discovering that someone's eyes were closed or the picture was blurry. Edwin Land thought this could be different, and the idea came from a small child.

Land was a brilliant American inventor. Born in 1909 in Bridgeport, Connecticut, he left Harvard University after his first year to work on his own experiments, and he invented cheap plastic sheets that polarize light, filtering out glare. These were used in sunglasses, camera filters and scientific instruments, and in 1937 he named his company Polaroid. The story he often told goes like this: during a family vacation in Santa Fe, New Mexico, in the 1940s, he took a picture of his three-year-old daughter Jennifer, and she asked why she could not see the photograph right away. Land later said that by the end of that day, he had worked out much of how an instant camera could work, though it took years of research to make it real.

On 21 February 1947, Land demonstrated his instant camera at a meeting of the Optical Society of America in New York, making a portrait of himself that appeared in about a minute. Then, in November 1948, the first Polaroid Land Camera, the Model 95, went on sale at Jordan Marsh, a department store in Boston, for 89.75 dollars. All 57 cameras the store had were sold on the first day.

How did it work? The camera held two rolls: a light-sensitive negative and a positive sheet of paper, plus a small sealed pod of thick, gooey chemicals. After you took a picture, you pulled the film out between two rollers. The rollers squeezed the pod, spreading the jelly evenly between the negative and the paper, like toothpaste squeezed into a sandwich. The chemicals developed the negative and, at the same time, moved silver to the paper to make a positive image. After about a minute, you opened a little door and peeled the finished picture away. The first prints were brownish, a color called sepia. Black-and-white prints followed, then Polacolor color film in 1963.

In 1972 Polaroid launched the SX-70, a folding camera that pushed out a print which developed by itself in front of your eyes, with no peeling at all. Instant cameras became party favorites, and many people loved watching a picture slowly appear. Land, who held 535 patents by the time he retired as Polaroid's chairman in 1982, called it his crowning achievement. Polaroid struggled in the digital age and stopped making film in 2008, but a group of fans called the Impossible Project rented part of an old Polaroid factory in the Netherlands and, from 2010, started making instant film again, and today instant cameras from Polaroid and Fujifilm's Instax line are popular once more.

sections.heading: Home Movies and Easy-Load Cameras
paragraphs: Ordinary families did not only want still photos. They wanted moving pictures of birthday parties, first steps and summer holidays. The problem was that professional 35mm movie film was expensive, and it was made of nitrate, which could catch fire easily. That was not something to keep in a family cupboard.

In 1923 Kodak introduced 16mm film for amateurs, along with the Ciné-Kodak camera and the Kodascope projector. The first outfit cost 335 dollars, a lot of money then, but 16mm film used a much safer acetate base that did not burn like nitrate. It also used reversal film, which turns directly into a positive picture after processing, so no separate print was needed. Wealthy families, schools, scientists and explorers loved it, and later TV news crews and even armies used 16mm for its light, portable cameras.

To make home movies cheaper, Kodak introduced 8mm film in 1932. It was a clever trick: the film was really 16mm wide, but the camera exposed pictures down only one half of the strip. Then you opened the camera, flipped the spool over, and filmed down the other half. After processing, the lab slit the film down the middle and joined the two halves into one long 8mm strip. Each frame was tiny, but it was good enough for a family screen, and it used much less film.

Threading film into a camera in the right way was fiddly, and mistakes could ruin a reel. So in 1965 Kodak launched Super 8, which came in a plastic cartridge you simply dropped into the camera. Its sprocket holes were smaller, leaving more room for a bigger picture. A cartridge lasted about three minutes of filming. From 1973, some Super 8 cameras could record sound too. Millions of families filmed their lives in Super 8 until video camcorders replaced it in the 1980s, and several famous film directors made their first movies on 8mm or Super 8 as children.

Still cameras got the same easy treatment. In 1963 Kodak introduced the Instamatic, which used a drop-in film cartridge called 126. The first models cost about 16 dollars, and more than 50 million Instamatics were made by 1970. In 1972 the smaller Pocket Instamatic, using 110 film, followed. Later came automatic point-and-shoot 35mm cameras that focused and set the exposure for you, and from the mid-1980s single-use cameras, cardboard boxes with film inside, that you could buy at a gas station and send back whole for developing. By the 1990s, taking pictures was something almost every family did without thinking twice.

sections.heading: Earth in the Viewfinder
paragraphs: The most important home photograph of all may have been taken about 380,000 kilometers from home. On 24 December 1968, three NASA astronauts, Frank Borman, Jim Lovell and Bill Anders, were orbiting the Moon in Apollo 8, the first time humans had ever traveled there. Their job included photographing the Moon's surface to help plan future landings. Then, as their spacecraft came around the Moon, Anders saw something nobody had seen with their own eyes before: Earth, blue and white, rising over the gray lunar horizon.

The crew scrambled for cameras. Anders first took a black-and-white picture, then asked for a color film magazine and took more. He used a modified Hasselblad camera, a Swedish medium-format camera, loaded with special Kodak Ektachrome color film. One of those color photographs, catalogued by NASA as AS08-14-2383, became known as Earthrise. In the original frame, Earth is to the side of the Moon, because in space there is no real up or down; the published version was rotated so that Earth seems to rise above the horizon, just as the Moon rises at home.

Earthrise showed our whole planet as small, beautiful and fragile, floating alone in the darkness of space. Anders later said the crew had gone to explore the Moon, and the most important thing they discovered was Earth. The nature photographer Galen Rowell called it the most influential environmental photograph ever taken. It appeared on a US postage stamp in 1969, and it is often credited with helping inspire the environmental movement, including the first Earth Day on 22 April 1970.

Four years later came another famous view. On 7 December 1972, the crew of Apollo 17, the last crewed mission to the Moon so far, photographed Earth from about 29,000 kilometers away as they headed out. Because the Sun was shining from behind them, almost the whole planet was lit up, like a full moon. The photograph, called The Blue Marble, shows Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Madagascar and the ice of Antarctica, with swirling white clouds. NASA credits the whole crew, Eugene Cernan, Ronald Evans and Harrison Schmitt, though evidence suggests Schmitt probably pressed the shutter. It became one of the most widely shared images in history.

Think how far photography had come. A century earlier, photographers hauled glass plates and darkroom wagons across battlefields. Now a camera only a little larger than a lunchbox had shown all of humanity what our home looks like from space.

By the end of the 20th century, cameras were everywhere: in handbags, on spacecraft, at birthday parties and in newsrooms. People trusted photographs. A picture in a newspaper or a family album felt like proof that something had really happened, just as it looked. But that trust had a weak spot. Ever since the 1800s, a few clever people had been discovering how easily a photograph could be staged, cut, painted over or combined with another, and how readily people would believe it. The next part asks a tricky question: can a picture lie?

deepDive: Many of the most influential photographs of the 20th century raise hard questions historians still discuss. Take Migrant Mother. Dorothea Lange's field notes and later accounts described the family as having sold their car tires to buy food and living on frozen vegetables and birds the children caught. Florence Owens Thompson's family later disputed parts of this; one of her sons said they had no tires to sell. Historians also note that the photo was carefully chosen and retouched (the thumb in the corner was removed), and that the FSA's photography project, led by Roy Stryker, selected images partly to win public support for government aid. None of this makes the picture fake, but it shows that documentary photographs are made by people with goals, and that the subjects often had little say in how their faces were used. Something similar applies to reformers like Jacob Riis, whose flash photos exposed real suffering but whose captions sometimes stereotyped the very people he photographed. On the technical side, the shift to 35mm involved a real trade-off. A 24 by 36 millimeter negative has far less area than a 4 by 5 inch sheet of film (about 864 square millimeters versus about 12,900), so enlargements show more grain and less fine detail. Photographers accepted that loss in exchange for speed, quietness and the ability to shoot dozens of frames quickly, and lens and film improvements steadily narrowed the gap. Flash technology also illustrates how speed is measured. A typical flashbulb burns for very roughly a fiftieth of a second, while Edgerton's electronic flashes could be shorter than a microsecond. Because motion blur depends on how far an object moves while the light is on, a bullet travelling hundreds of meters per second moves less than a millimeter during a sub-microsecond flash, which is why it appears frozen. Finally, the space photos remind us that crediting a photograph can be complicated: Frank Borman at first said he had taken the black-and-white Earthrise frame before agreeing that Anders took all of them, and NASA still credits The Blue Marble to the whole Apollo 17 crew.
funFact: All 57 Polaroid Land Cameras that the Jordan Marsh department store in Boston had for the first day of sale in November 1948 sold out that same day.

check.q: What simple idea let Oskar Barnack make the Leica camera so small?
check.a: He used 35mm movie film, running it sideways to make 24 x 36 mm pictures
